abstract: Existing real-world reinforcement learning methods improve robot policies by combining human corrections with autonomous rollouts. However, accumulated experience varies in its value for policy improvement, and even successful trajectories can contain inefficient or redundant behavior, motivating more selective experience reuse. To this end, we propose Evo-RL, an iterative reinforcement learning method that combines human interventions with advantage-guided experience selection. Evo-RL uses human corrections and experience with positive estimated advantages from successful trajectories to iteratively refine the policy. To support learning from these different experience sources, we introduce RW-RL-Dataset, which spans over 1,000 hours across four robot embodiments. On a real-world high-precision manipulation task, Evo-RL improves attempt success rate over RECAP by 30.46%. Our code, model checkpoints, and dataset are publicly available.

sections.body: Robot policies trained on demonstrations can meet unfamiliar states and fail to recover. RECAP combines demonstrations, autonomous rollouts, and human interventions, but this paper argues that the value of experience varies within trajectories, and that even successful trajectories can contain inefficient behavior. Evo-RL starts from a demonstration-trained policy and collects interventions and autonomous rollouts. It trains a value model with rewards that account for execution time and human takeovers, then estimates advantages. For fine-tuning, it keeps only the human-controlled portions of successful intervention trajectories, keeps the original demonstrations, and adds selected positive-advantage experience. The paper reports a 30.46% higher attempt success rate than RECAP on a high-precision manipulation task, and introduces RW-RL-Dataset, which spans over 1,000 hours across four robot embodiments.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing methods reuse experience unevenly, so Evo-RL selects experience by estimated advantage and retains only human-controlled intervention segments.

sections.body: The section reviews VLA pretraining datasets, DAgger-style aggregation of expert labels on policy-visited states, and intervention-weighted methods such as IWR. It notes that corrective action labels alone do not indicate which states lead to failure or which trajectories are of higher quality. It describes GRAPE, which uses Direct Preference Optimization for offline alignment, RECAP, which conditions training on value-based advantage indicators, RLT, which trains a lightweight actor-critic on an RL token while the VLA stays frozen, and LaST-R1, which extends reinforcement learning to the latent space. The authors state that Evo-RL is motivated by RECAP because both combine human corrections with autonomous rollouts for value-guided iterative improvement. The section reports no experiments.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work pairs human corrections with offline alignment or value-guided updates, but corrective data is still poorly organized.

sections.body: The policy takes camera images, proprioceptive state, and an instruction, and outputs action chunks with a flow-matching objective. Intervention data keeps only human-controlled frames from successful trajectories, so policy-controlled actions are excluded. Each nonterminal frame receives reward -1, and a takeover adds a penalty of `C_int` to the transition before it. The terminal frame has reward 0. A vision-only value model predicts a categorical distribution over 201 bins evenly spaced in [-1, 0], and its scalar estimate is the probability-weighted mean of the bin centers. Advantages use a lookahead of at most n frames, bounded by the chunk length. Positive-advantage segments from demonstrations and successful autonomous rollouts are then selected for sampling. The section reports no quantitative results.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Evo-RL initializes from demonstrations, then trains a value model on time and takeover costs and selects positive-advantage segments for fine-tuning.

sections.body: The dataset contains more than 1,000 hours of real-world interaction on AgiBot G2, Galaxea R1Lite, AgileX PiperX, and SO-101. Each platform has its own sensor set, including multiple RGB streams and wrist views, and PiperX and SO-101 are dual-arm systems with 14-dimensional and 12-dimensional state and action vectors. The data cover nine scene domains and more than 30 task templates, such as object sorting, precision insertion, and garment folding. Episodes are labeled as teleoperated demonstrations, autonomous policy rollouts, or human-intervention episodes. Annotations exist at dataset, episode, and frame levels, and frame-level controller labels identify human and policy actions. All annotations share a unified timestamp system.
sections.heading: RW-RL-Dataset
sections.headline: RW-RL-Dataset spans over 1,000 hours across four robot embodiments, with three-level semantic annotations and action-source metadata.

sections.body: Experiments use PiperX insertion and SO-101 folding, with a five-minute limit per trial. Under matched budgets from 2 h to 16 h, replacing one hour of demonstrations with human-intervention data raises attempt success rate from 27.03% to 51.52% at 4 h. The 8 h mixture reaches 78.00%, close to 78.26% for 16 h of demonstrations only. On PiperX, first-round Evo-RL reaches 88.24%, compared with 78.72% for SFT with interventions and 57.78% for RECAP, and a second round reaches 92.16%. On SO-101 folding, Evo-RL raises attempt success rate from 55.56% to 76.67%. The value model is a vision-only SigLIP encoder with an MLP head. Comparisons use N=10 planned instances per PiperX unit and N=20 per folding stage.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: On PiperX, first-round Evo-RL reaches 88.24% attempt success against 57.78% for RECAP, and a second round reaches 92.16%.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes Evo-RL as combining human corrections with advantage-guided experience selection in an iterative loop. It states that interventions outperform additional demonstrations under matched human-control budgets, and that Evo-RL improves attempt success rate and throughput on high-precision and deformable-object manipulation tasks. On PiperX, it outperforms RECAP and either update stage alone, with further gains in a second iteration. RW-RL-Dataset is presented as bringing together demonstrations, interventions, and autonomous experience, including the training data used in the evaluation.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Evo-RL is concluded to outperform RECAP on PiperX, and RW-RL-Dataset is presented as a combined collection of experience.
